questions.text:
Consider a schedule of transactions T1 and T2:

Here, RX stands for "Read(X)" and WX stands for "Write(X)". Which one of the following schedules is conflict equivalent to the above schedule?
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs in the given schedule (their order must be kept):
- B: [latex]T_2[/latex]'s RB, WB come before [latex]T_1[/latex]'s WB
- C: [latex]T_1[/latex]'s RC comes before [latex]T_2[/latex]'s WC
- D: [latex]T_2[/latex]'s RD comes before [latex]T_1[/latex]'s WD

Schedule (A): [latex]T_2[/latex]: RB WB RD, then [latex]T_1[/latex]: RA RC WD WB, then [latex]T_2[/latex]: WC. All three orders are kept True. The other schedules reverse at least one pair.

Answer: A

questions.text: Consider a relational table R that is in 3NF, but not in BCNF. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
3NF allows [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex] with X not a superkey only when A is a prime attribute. BCNF forbids it.

So a relation in 3NF but not in BCNF must have such an FD with prime A. The other options describe 3NF/2NF violations or a 1NF violation.

Answer: X [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] A where X is not a superkey and A is a prime attribute

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a prime attribute.
R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a non-prime attribute and X is not a proper subset of any key.
R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a non-prime attribute and X is a proper subset of some key.
A cell in R holds a set instead of an atomic value.

questions.text: Which one of the following is used to represent the supporting many-one relationships of a weak entity set in an entity-relationship diagram?
questions.solution:
The relationship that links a weak entity to its owner (the identifying relationship) is drawn as a diamond with a double border. The weak entity itself is a double rectangle.

Answer: Diamonds with double/bold border

questions.text:
Consider a relational database containing the following schemas.

The primary key of each table is indicated by underlining the constituent fields. 
 SELECT s.sno, s.sname
    FROM Suppliers s, Catalogue c
    WHERE s.sno=c.sno AND
        cost > (SELECT AVG (cost)
                FROM Catalogue
                WHERE pno = 'P4'
                GROUP BY pno) ;

The number of rows returned by the above SQL query is
questions.solution:
Subquery: average cost of P4 = (200 + 250) / 2 = 225.

Catalogue rows with cost [latex]\gt[/latex] 225: (S2, P5, 250), (S3, P1, 250), (S3, P5, 300), (S3, P4, 250) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 rows.

Each joins with exactly one supplier, and there is no DISTINCT, so 4 rows are returned.

Answer: 4

questions.text:
Consider the following relation P(X, Y, Z), Q(X, Y, T) and R(Y, V):

How many tuples will be returned by the following relational algebra query?

Answer:______
questions.solution:
Left part: R tuples with V = V2 are (Y3, V2) and (Y2, V2). P has Y = Y2 only in (X2, Y2, Z2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {X2}.
Right part: Q tuples with T [latex]\gt[/latex] 2 are (X1, Y2, 5) and (X1, Y1, 6); both Y2 and Y1 exist in R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {X1}.

{X2} [latex]-[/latex] {X1} = {X2} [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 tuple.

Answer: 1
